title: What is `coalesce(n, shuffle=true)` and why is it equivalent to `repartition(n)`?
shortTitle: `coalesce(n, shuffle=true)` — why it becomes equivalent to `repartition(n)`

s1_definition.profdef: `coalesce(n)` by default is a narrow transformation that reduces the number of partitions without a shuffle by stitching adjacent partitions together on the same executor. When you pass the optional shuffle flag as true, `coalesce(n, shuffle=true)`, it inserts a full shuffle stage before the merge, which gives it round-robin redistribution into exactly `n` partitions. That behaviour is identical to `repartition(n)`, and in fact `repartition(n)` is implemented internally as `coalesce(n, shuffle=true)`.
s1_definition.analogy: Normal coalesce is like telling two neighbouring clerks at the National Bank of India "combine your two stacks of slips into one" — no slips travel across the room, they just merge what is already next to them. But `coalesce` with the shuffle flag on is like first collecting every slip into the middle of the room and re-dealing them evenly to `n` clerks. That re-dealing is a shuffle, and re-dealing evenly into `n` stacks is precisely what repartition does.
s1_definition.oneliner: `coalesce(n, shuffle=true)` turns the cheap no-shuffle merge into a full shuffle, which is exactly how `repartition(n)` is built.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `coalesce(n)` by default is a narrow transformation that reduces the number of partitions without a shuffle by stitching adjacent partitions together on the same executor. When you pass the optional shuffle flag as true, `coalesce(n, shuffle=true)`, it inserts a full shuffle stage before the merge, which gives it round-robin redistribution into exactly `n` partitions. That behaviour is identical to `repartition(n)`, and in fact `repartition(n)` is implemented internally as `coalesce(n, shuffle=true)`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Normal coalesce is like telling two neighbouring clerks at the National Bank of India "combine your two stacks of slips into one" — no slips travel across the room, they just merge what is already next to them. But `coalesce` with the shuffle flag on is like first collecting every slip into the middle of the room and re-dealing them evenly to `n` clerks. That re-dealing is a shuffle, and re-dealing evenly into `n` stacks is precisely what repartition does.

**One line to remember:** `coalesce(n, shuffle=true)` turns the cheap no-shuffle merge into a full shuffle, which is exactly how `repartition(n)` is built.

sections.s2_technical:
By default, `coalesce(n)` avoids a shuffle. Spark marks the dependency as narrow and simply groups existing partitions so that several parents feed one child partition on the same executor. This is cheap but has two limits: it can only decrease the count, and the resulting partitions are as uneven as the originals were.

When you set the shuffle flag to true, Spark can no longer use the narrow path. It inserts an exchange (shuffle) that redistributes records round-robin. The code path is the same one `repartition` uses, which is why the two are equivalent. Concretely, in the Spark source, `repartition(numPartitions)` calls `coalesce(numPartitions, shuffle = true)`. So any claim you make about `repartition(n)` — even balance, ability to increase the count, cost of a full shuffle — applies identically to `coalesce(n, shuffle=true)`.

The reason you would ever write `coalesce(n, shuffle=true)` instead of `repartition(n)` is mostly historical or for explicitness in an existing coalesce-based code path. There is also a subtle use: when you are reducing from a very large number of partitions down to a small number but the upstream computation is expensive, a plain `coalesce` would collapse the upstream parallelism (because the narrow dependency pushes the small partition count up the chain). Passing shuffle=true breaks that chain with an exchange, letting the upstream stage keep its high parallelism and only the final stage run with `n` partitions. In that scenario the shuffle is a feature, not a cost to avoid.

A senior-level nuance is understanding why `coalesce(n)` (no shuffle) to a smaller number can reduce upstream parallelism: because there is no shuffle boundary, the task that produces the coalesced partition also runs the upstream transformations, so collapsing to one partition can force the whole upstream computation into a single task. Adding shuffle=true inserts the boundary and prevents that.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a daily settlement job that reads 200 partitions of trades, runs an expensive enrichment per record, and must write a small number of output files. The engineer writes `coalesce(4)` to reduce to four files. But because plain coalesce has no shuffle boundary, the expensive enrichment collapses to run inside only four tasks, so the job slows to a crawl. This is exactly where `coalesce(4, shuffle=true)` helps — it inserts a shuffle so the enrichment keeps running across 200 tasks, and only the final write stage uses four partitions.

Problem 2 — Another engineer wants perfectly even output files. Plain coalesce stitches uneven partitions, so the four files come out lopsided. `coalesce(4, shuffle=true)` re-deals round-robin into four even partitions, which is identical to `repartition(4)`.

The demo models a pipeline stage count and shows how plain coalesce pushes the small count upstream (reducing parallelism) while coalesce-with-shuffle inserts a boundary that preserves upstream parallelism and balances the output — proving the equivalence to repartition.

java -cp target/spark-coalesce-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.spark.CoalesceDemo

#   df.coalesce(4)                 # narrow, no shuffle, may collapse upstream parallelism

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a settlement job starting with 200 trade partitions that needs 4 output files after an expensive enrichment.

Step 1: The planner evaluates plain `coalesce(4)`. Because there is no shuffle boundary, the target count of four is pushed up the dependency chain, so the expensive enrichment is forced to run inside only four tasks. The plan reports upstream parallelism of four — a performance problem.

Step 2: The planner evaluates `coalesce(4, shuffle=true)`. A shuffle exchange is inserted between the enrichment stage and the output stage. The enrichment keeps all 200 tasks, and only the final stage runs with four partitions. The plan reports upstream parallelism of 200 and output of four.

Step 3: The planner evaluates `repartition(4)`. Internally this is the same call as coalesce with the shuffle flag, so it produces an identical plan.

Step 4: The demo compares the two plans field by field and confirms they are equal, proving the equivalence.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 04:21:10 [WARNING] coalesce(4): upstream parallelism collapses to 4 tasks — expensive work runs in only 4 tasks!
2026-10-30 04:21:10 [INFO] coalesce(4, shuffle=true): upstream keeps 200 tasks, output = 4 files
2026-10-30 04:21:10 [INFO] repartition(4) plan equals coalesce(4, shuffle=true) plan? true
2026-10-30 04:21:10 [INFO] Proven: repartition(n) IS coalesce(n, shuffle=true).
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
By default, coalesce is a narrow transformation that reduces partitions without a shuffle by stitching existing partitions together on the same executor. It is cheap, but it can only decrease the count and it leaves partitions uneven. The optional second argument, the shuffle flag, changes everything: when it is true, Spark inserts a full shuffle exchange and redistributes records round-robin into exactly the number of partitions requested. That is identical to repartition, and the equivalence is literal — in the Spark source, repartition with a number simply calls coalesce with that number and the shuffle flag set to true.

The practical reason the shuffle flag matters is upstream parallelism. Plain coalesce has no shuffle boundary, so the small target partition count is pushed up the dependency chain, and any expensive computation above the coalesce is forced to run in that small number of tasks. Setting the shuffle flag inserts a boundary that decouples the stages, so the expensive work keeps its full parallelism and only the final stage runs with the reduced count.

In my settlement job at the National Bank of India I hit exactly this. We read two hundred partitions of trades, ran an expensive enrichment, and wanted four output files. Writing plain coalesce of four collapsed the enrichment into four tasks and the job crawled. Switching to coalesce of four with the shuffle flag kept the enrichment running across two hundred tasks and only reduced to four at write time, which is the same as writing repartition of four. So my rule is that coalesce without shuffle is the cheap merge for when upstream parallelism does not matter, and coalesce with the shuffle flag is just another name for repartition, which I use when I need a shuffle boundary or even output.
